findings.summary: M4.35's new sentence -- the one this round added to retire the 'only on a future S3 backend' hedge -- is FALSE against the backends that exist, and I measured it both ways. It reads: 'That write is interruptible ON THE BACKEND THAT EXISTS TODAY, not only on a future S3 one: LocalFsBinStore.putIfMatch goes through Files.createTempFile and Files.copy(InputStream, Path, ...), and putIfAbsent opens an explicit FileChannel, whose AbstractInterruptibleChannel.begin() throws ClosedByInterruptException when the flag is ALREADY SET on entry ... So the write dies with ClosedByInterruptException.' The write under discussion is releaseLocked()'s (LeaseManager.java:453: store.putIfMatch(key, Body.ofBytes(expired.encode()), mine.version())). putIfMatch (LocalFsBinStore.java:224-259) opens NO channel: it is Files.exists / readMeta(Files.readString) / Files.createTempFile / Files.copy(InputStream, Path, REPLACE_EXISTING) / moveAtomically / writeMeta(Files.writeString). None of those are interruptible -- Files.newOutputStream returns an UNINTERRUPTIBLE FileChannel, so begin()/end() never fire. Measured on this tree's JDK 25 (Temurin 25.0.4), flag pre-set, platform and virtual thread alike: Files.copy(InputStream, Path, REPLACE_EXISTING) COMPLETED with the flag still set; Files.writeString COMPLETED; only the explicit FileChannel.open(...CREATE_NEW, WRITE) form threw ClosedByInterruptException. Then end-to-end against the real class: new LocalFsBinStore(tmp).putIfMatch("ctl/lease/0.json", Body.ofBytes(...), v) on a virtual thread with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() set on entry returned Optional[Version[token=2]] and the file on disk held the new content -- i.e. the release SUCCEEDS. The other existing backend, MemoryBinStore, does no I/O at all, and binstore-backends/src/main/java/binjava/binstore/backend/ contains only those two. The defect is the clause-attachment the packet warns about: 'whose AbstractInterruptibleChannel.begin()' attaches to putIfAbsent's FileChannel, and putIfAbsent is NOT on the release path -- the conclusion 'So the write dies' is then drawn about putIfMatch, which has no channel. (Secondary, subsumed: begin() does not itself throw ClosedByInterruptException; it closes the channel and end() throws.) The row's HEADLINE survives via its other branch -- 'under lock contention takeOrFail throws at once' is real (LeaseManager.release() line 419-421 -> BoundedLock.tryLock(bound, NANOSECONDS)) -- so the remedy is to restore the S3-contingent framing of the ClosedByInterruptException branch (or delete that branch and rest the row on takeOrFail), not to drop M4.35.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.35 lands in the authoritative task list asserting, in the present tense, a hazard branch that does not exist at HEAD -- non-negotiable 4, in the one commit whose entire deliverable is the truth of these rows, and asserted here precisely as a CORRECTION of a hedge that was accurate. Whoever picks M4.35 up writes the obvious characterisation test -- pin the committer inside closeDelegateQuietly's delegate.close(), interrupt it, assert the LocalFsBinStore-backed release fails -- and it will never go red, because the release completes. They then either conclude the hazard is imaginary and close the row (losing the takeOrFail branch, which IS real), or hunt for the missing ClosedByInterruptException in production code that cannot produce it. The row also becomes the citation any later reader trusts for 'today's backend does interruptible channel I/O on the lease path', which is false and would mis-scope any future interrupt-safety audit.

findings.summary: The done-row's closing clause inverts the very mislabelling it is retiring, and drags a relative clause onto the wrong noun while doing it: 'the 200ms-constant mutation M4.37 disputes was measured LANDING at ~202-211ms ... -- a margin of ~90-100ms, which is the quantity two drafts of these rows mislabelled as the measurement itself'. (a) 'which' attaches to 'a margin of ~90-100ms', so the sentence claims the drafts labelled the MARGIN as the measurement. They did the opposite: the prior done-row said 'the margin M4.37 disputes was measured at 203,911,796 ns' -- it labelled the MEASUREMENT (the mutant's elapsed time) as the margin. No draft ever wrote 90-100ms at all. M4.37's own row (backlog-notes.md:297) states the direction correctly ('THAT IS THE MUTANT'S ELAPSED TIME, NOT THE MARGIN'), so the two rows in this one commit describe the same history in opposite directions. (b) 'the 200ms-constant mutation M4.37 disputes' -- M4.37 does not dispute the mutation; it asserts it as evidence. What M4.37 disputes is the '~400 ms of slack' figure in the test comment. The 'M4.37 disputes' clause is a leftover from the previous draft, where it correctly modified 'the margin', and re-attaching it to 'the mutation' makes it false. The NUMBERS themselves check out: measured here, the 200ms-constant window elapses 200.7-201.1 ms against the 300 ms floor (margin ~99 ms) and the 4x mutant 1201 ms, so ~202-211ms / ~90-100ms are honest figures.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader of the done-row learns the opposite of the correction the commit exists to make, in the sentence advertised as making it -- and since the done-row is the durable record (backlog-notes.md's M4.37 row disappears when M4.37 lands), the surviving account of what went wrong will be the inverted one. A later editor reconciling the two rows will 'fix' the correct one to match.

findings.summary: 'the close()-interrupts-its-own-release hazard, the join-timeout WARNING and its undetected drain net, and the two unpinned M4.7 changes are filed; the awaitSet-polls-where-a-latch-would-be-exact minor is DELIBERATELY NOT, since baselines/review.txt records only the first as belonging in a row.' 'The first' resolves, for any reader, against the three-item list it immediately follows -- i.e. 'only the close()-interrupts-its-own-release hazard belongs in a row', which contradicts this same commit filing M4.36 and M4.37. The intended referent is the first of the TWO minors in baselines/review.txt's closing sentence ('only one of the two drain nets is pinned ... and awaitSet polls where a latch would be exact. The first is a design signal about that constant and belongs in a row'), i.e. the drain net -- which is the SECOND item in the row's own list. The justification is sound; the pronoun points at the wrong list.
findings.failure_scenario: The one sentence explaining why a known minor was deliberately not filed reads, on its plain construction, as a statement that two of the three rows this commit files should not exist either. A reader checking whether the filing is complete cannot resolve it without opening baselines/review.txt and reverse-engineering which enumeration 'the first' indexes.

findings.summary: M4.36's new paragraph ends 'aQUEUEDCallerIsFailedWithoutWaitingForTheLeaseReleaseToFinish already uses an interrupt-insensitive spin for the same reason'. The spin is real (BatchingSequencerTerminationTest.java:314-320, a Thread.onSpinWait loop on queuedCount()), but not for that reason: that test's own comment says the spin exists so the delegate dies only once caller B is really queued -- batch-membership determinism -- and nothing interrupts the committer there before it throws its OutOfMemoryError, so interrupt-insensitivity is never exercised. The precedent cited is a coincidence of mechanism, not of motive. The MECHANISM claim the sentence supports is correct and I reproduced it: with close()'s failAll(drainRemaining(), terminalFailure()) deleted, a CountDownLatch.await() pin lets the queued caller be freed anyway (mutation SURVIVES: caller B got 'IOException: this sequencer is closed' under both original and mutant) while a Semaphore.acquireUninterruptibly() pin leaves B parked past 2.5s under the mutant and freed under the original (mutation KILLED).
findings.failure_scenario: Whoever builds M4.36's test reads 'for the same reason' and copies the existing spin believing it is already an interrupt-proof precedent, rather than understanding that the interrupt-proofing is a NEW requirement this test introduces. Since a wrong pin makes the test pass while pinning nothing -- exactly what this paragraph exists to prevent -- an appeal to a precedent that does not carry the property is the wrong thing for that reader to lean on.
